messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Estimating abundance from acoustic data
parts:
We faced this same problem with double-counting in bats and N-mixture, using Royle's model in our counts at Mammoth Cave, which have not yet been published. We developed a workaround for the problem, but I can't imagine how it could be applied to acoustic data (ours are images at emergence). There are some Bayesian abundance models of Kery's that could accommodate double-counting. Double-counting is treated as an allocation error (false positive) in these. On the other hand, you might consider using Royle's abundance dependent occupancy or that of Miller (which is robust to allocation error). Both are implemented in unmarked. If you have a lot of data and are working at regional scales, these might work for you. You lose some information by reducing the counts to occupancy, but they are fairly robust to violations that sink N-mixture.

Tom Ingersoll, PhD
Mathematician

On Friday, November 26, 2021, 09:52:29 AM EST, Carlos Henrique Russi <carlosh...@gmail.com> wrote:


Hi everyone.

I'm developing a project whose objective is to estimate the abundance (correcting for detectability) of bats at different elevations and seasons. For sampling, I will use ultrasound recorders, which will be installed at each location for 6 consecutive nights in each season of the year (summer, autumn, etc.), resulting in 24 nights of sampling per location (6 nights * 4 seasons).

In my view, the Dail and Mansen N-mixture open population model (pcountOpen function) would be the natural alternative to analyze such data, as it would allow me to model both the initial abundance of each location and the population dynamics throughout the year.

However, my data has a problem that I believe cannot be detected by such models: the same bat will certainly be detected numerous times in the same night. Through my data it is impossible to distinguish if, for example, 10 records come from 10 individuals detected once each, or only 1 individual detected 10 times.

In this context, my questions are:
(1) Am I right in thinking that the Dail and Mansen model is not capable of dealing with such a problem?
(2) Are there any alternatives in unmarked package to model abundance and detectability when an (unmarked) individual can be detected multiple times in the same sample?

--
